				function getOverlayMessage(platform, platformName, privacyPolicyLink, foundryPPLink, callback, cmpType) {
					let customHTMLTextOverlay = window?.IDG?.settings?.overlays_privacy_policies?.consent_overlays?.english_overlay_message ?? '';
					customHTMLTextOverlay = customHTMLTextOverlay.replace(/\$\{platformName\}/g, platformName).replace(/\$\{privacyPolicyLink\}/g, privacyPolicyLink).replace(/\$\{foundryPPLink\}/g, foundryPPLink).replace(/\$\{platform\}/g, platform).replace(/\$\{callback\}/g, callback).replace(/\$\{cmp\}/g, cmpType);
					return customHTMLTextOverlay;
				}
				function setOverlayCookie(name, value, days) {
					let expires = "";
					if (days) {
						const date = new Date();
						date.setTime(date.getTime() + (days * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000));
						expires = "; expires=" + date.toUTCString();
					}
					document.cookie = name + "=" + (value || "") + expires + "; path=/";
				}
				function getOverlayCookie(name) {
					const nameEQ = name + "=";
					const ca = document.cookie.split(';');
					for(let i = 0; i < ca.length; i++) {
						let c = ca[i];
						while (c.charAt(0) === ' ') c = c.substring(1, c.length);
						if (c.indexOf(nameEQ) === 0) return c.substring(nameEQ.length, c.length);
					}
					return null;
				}
				function renderOverlay(element, platform, platformName, ppLink, foundryPPLink, callback, cmpType) {
					const cookieName = `hide-overlay-${platform}`;
					const consentGiven = getOverlayCookie(cookieName);
					console.log('[Consent] renderOverlay cookieName %s consent given %s',cookieName, consentGiven);
					if (consentGiven !== 'true') {
						const overlayNextExists = jQuery(element).next(`.${cookieName}`).length > 0;
						const overlayPrevExists = jQuery(element).prev(`.${cookieName}`).length > 0;
						if (!overlayNextExists && !overlayPrevExists) {
							const textOverlay = getOverlayMessage(platform, platformName, ppLink, foundryPPLink, callback, cmpType);
							jQuery(textOverlay).insertAfter(element);
							jQuery(element).hide();
						}
					} else {
						jQuery(element).show();
						//eval(callback);
						window[callback.split('(')[0]]();//dont think any of the have actual arguments
						const src = element.getAttribute('src');
						const dataSrc = element.getAttribute('data-src');
						console.log('[Consent] renderOverlay src %s dataSrc %s',src, dataSrc);
						if (dataSrc ) {
							element.setAttribute('src', dataSrc); // Move data-src to src
						}
					}
				}
				function showOverlays(cmpType) {
					console.log('[Consent] showOverlays cmpType ',cmpType);
					const blocksForConsent = window?.blocksForConsent ?? [];
					Object.entries(blocksForConsent).forEach(function([key, value]) {
						//key = slideshare, twitter etc
						const { platform, platformName, selector, privacyPolicyLink, callback } = value;
						const elements = document.querySelectorAll(`${selector}`);
						// selector for iframes and scripts within 'legacy_content' for the custom blcok.
						const legacySelector = `.legacy_content iframe[data-src*="${platform}"], .legacy_content script[src*="${platform}"], .legacy_content script[data-src*="${platform}"], .legacy_content blockquote[class*="${platform}"]`;
						// Select all iframes and scripts within the div with class 'legacy_content' that match the dynamic selectors.
						const legacyElements = document.querySelectorAll(legacySelector);
						const ppLink = window?.IDG?.settings?.overlays_privacy_policies?.[privacyPolicyLink]?.[cmpType];
						const foundryPPLink = window?.IDG?.settings?.overlays_privacy_policies?.foundry_privacy_policies?.[cmpType];

						elements.forEach(function(element) {
							renderOverlay(element, platform, platformName, ppLink, foundryPPLink, callback, cmpType)
						});
						legacyElements.forEach(function(element) {
							renderOverlay(element, platform, platformName, ppLink, foundryPPLink, `renderCustomBlockInLegacyContent('${platform}', '${callback}')`, cmpType);
						});
					});
				}

<p class="wp-block-paragraph">For several years now I’ve complained about the fact that basic iPhones, despite costing less, come with much nicer colors than their Pro equivalents. <a href="https://www.macworld.com/article/2465458/why-cant-apples-pro-users-have-fun-too.html">Why can’t Pro users have fun too?</a></p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Perhaps Apple heard me, because last year’s Pro-exclusive Cosmic Orange was arguably Apple’s funnest color yet. (I’m using that word deliberately to prepare readers for the likely grammatical crimes of today’s Apple event.) But if the pre-launch rumors are true, that was only the precursor for a huge anti-fun announcement today.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The iPhone 18 Pro, <a href="https://www.macworld.com/article/3116701/iphone-18-pro-colors-revealed-exclusive-look-at-apples-2026-models.html">according to our sources</a>, will come in black, silver, light blue, and a charming burgundy branded as Dark Cherry. Less fun, arguably, than the green, blue, and lilac which the iPhone 17 will continue to offer (because its successor won’t arrive until the spring). But infinitely more fun than the poor iPhone Ultra/Duo, which is expected to come in just two colors: <a href="https://go.skimresources.com?id=111346X1569486&xs=1&url=https://x.com/markgurman/status/2097685704826581032&xcust=1-0-3228054-1-0-0-0-0&sref=https://www.macworld.com/article/3228054/surprise-and-shine-apple-event-live-blog-iphone-18-pro-folding-duo-airpods.html" rel="nofollow" data-subtag="1-0-3228054-1-0-0-0-0" data-domain-name="x" target="_blank">dark blue, and white</a>. Despite starting at $2,000, and going all the way up to $3,000 if you want the top storage tiers.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The more you pay, the less fun you get. Make it make sense, Apple.</p>

<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Forget iPhone Ultra, forget iPhone Fold… the latest breaking news is that Apple’s first ever folding handset will be called the <strong>iPhone Duo</strong>. That’s according to Mark Gurman’s sources, and he’s generally well informed when it comes to information like this.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Gurman made his last-minute prediction in an <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-09/apple-event-details-2-000-iphone-duo-apple-watch-series-12-recording-feature" rel="nofollow" data-subtag="1-0-3228054-1-0-0-0-0" data-domain-name="bloomberg" target="_blank">article</a> (subscription required) this morning. He also claimed the device will start at $2,000, have a short-and-wide design, and go on sale in October, later than the other new iPhones. But we knew all that already. The name is the real bombshell.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Some may accuse Apple of copying Microsoft, whose Surface Duo was a pioneer in this field. On the other hand, maybe Microsoft should have kept that brand going; the line was <a href="https://go.skimresources.com?id=111346X1569486&xs=1&url=https://www.windowscentral.com/phones/the-surface-duo-is-dead-microsoft-pulls-plug-on-usd1-500-surface-duo-2-after-just-one-android-os-upgrade&xcust=1-0-3228054-1-0-0-0-0&sref=https://www.macworld.com/article/3228054/surprise-and-shine-apple-event-live-blog-iphone-18-pro-folding-duo-airpods.html" rel="nofollow" data-subtag="1-0-3228054-1-0-0-0-0" data-domain-name="windowscentral" target="_blank">discontinued</a> nearly two years ago. The Duo brand also goes rather nicely with Neo, as in MacBook. And, please note, it was one of the options mentioned by my colleague Emma Rowley <a href="https://www.techadvisor.com/article/3216596/what-will-be-the-final-name-for-apples-iphone-ultra.html">earlier this week</a>.</p>

<p class="wp-block-paragraph">With less than a day to go before the keynote kicks off, there’s an interesting development concerning the Apple Watch SE 3. Over at Apple.com, every possible combination is listed as “currently unavailable” for delivery or pickup. And if you order one at Amazon, you won’t get a delivery date. That’s strange.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">For comparison, you can order a Series 11 or Ultra 3 without a problem. <p class="wp-block-paragraph">“We have great respect for these words,” said Tim Cook in 2017, “and we don’t use them lightly.” Those words, of course, were One More Thing.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">That <a href="https://www.macworld.com/article/674643/every-one-more-thing-apple-has-ever-announced.html">little phrase</a> has signalled the arrival of some of Apple’s most iconic products and services, including the iMac G4, the MacBook Pro, FaceTime, the Apple Watch, Apple Music, and the iPhone X. Will it be uttered this year, and if so, what will it herald?</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">We <a href="https://go.skimresources.com?id=111346X1569486&xs=1&url=https://www.tiktok.com/@macworld.com/video/7680990322582654238&xcust=1-0-3228054-1-0-0-0-0&sref=https://www.macworld.com/article/3228054/surprise-and-shine-apple-event-live-blog-iphone-18-pro-folding-duo-airpods.html" rel="nofollow" data-subtag="1-0-3228054-1-0-0-0-0" data-domain-name="tiktok" target="_blank">discussed this</a> on the podcast, and figured it would be a nice moment if new CEO John Ternus got the chance to utter those immortal words as part of his debut. (Debut as overall event host, that is. He’s spoken in individual segments before now.) The most obvious product to get the One More Thing treatment is the iPhone Ultra, but a bigger surprise would be the arrival of Apple’s long-rumored smart home hub. Either would work.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">But Macworld readers put forward other ideas. At the less serious end, <strong>jimrock</strong> reckoned “It’d be really sick if he announced a $2,000 monitor stand” while <strong>Adam Moran</strong> proposed “One more thing: Now shipping iPhones with a charger.” Hashtag courage.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Moving on to things that could happen (but won’t), <strong>Rob K</strong> put forward “One more thing: iPhone Air 2 with 6,000 mAh silicon carbon battery, three cameras, and no stupid fold.” And <strong>Tower Lord</strong> suggested “AI-driven smart glasses. Minus the creep factor found in Meta glasses. Instead, true spatial computing. The ultimate personal computer.” Get rid of the AI part and we’re on board.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">And finally, a note of sanity from <strong>Mike</strong>: “One more thing was Steve’s thing. Can we please stop measuring every CEO against Steve and let them be their own leaders?”</p>

<p class="wp-block-paragraph">When Apple (allegedly) unveils its first folding iPhone tomorrow, Greg Joswiak or whomever gets the honor of announcing the phone on the stream, will talk about the displays, interface, cameras, design, and anything else Apple feels is worth highlighting. What they probably won’t spend a lot of time talking about is the crease.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Ever since Samsung’s <a href="https://www.pcworld.com/article/403578/samsung-galaxy-fold-hands-on-roundup.html" data-type="link" data-id="https://www.pcworld.com/article/403578/samsung-galaxy-fold-hands-on-roundup.html">first folding phone arrived</a>, the center display crease has been an issue. It’s gotten better over the years, but it’s still the biggest hurdle for new customers to overcome. Even on the newest phones, you can see it when it’s opened and feel a little valley while using it. It’s flies in the face of Apple’s pursuit of perfection and likely the reason why we haven’t gotten a folding iPhone until now.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Earlier this year, it was <a href="https://www.macworld.com/article/3114106/new-report-explains-how-apple-will-solve-the-iphone-folds-crease-problem.html" data-type="link" data-id="https://www.macworld.com/article/3114106/new-report-explains-how-apple-will-solve-the-iphone-folds-crease-problem.html">reported that Apple had devised a way</a> to overcome the crease with a combination of ultra-thin glass (UTG) and an optically clear adhesive that allows “the folding area to be locally thinned at the bending axis to improve bendability.” Samsung’s newest flagship phone features a display with a 60-micrometer UTG layer, which is likely a similar material to what Apple will use. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">No folding phone has been able to completely eliminate the crease. Will Apple be the first?</p>

<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Sad to say for an event with the word surprise in its tagline, but there don’t seem to be many mysteries left concerning the foldable iPhone. With one notable exception: its name.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In the early days, most pundits referred to the rumored device as the <strong>iPhone Fold</strong> for obvious, logical reasons. But in the spring, we all started calling it the <strong>iPhone Ultra</strong>, even though, features-wise, that <a href="https://www.macworld.com/article/3225557/why-apples-folding-iphone-will-be-ultra-in-name-only.html">doesn’t entirely make sense</a>. <p class="wp-block-paragraph">Last year, the iPhone 17 Pro Max and iPhone Air competed for the title of Apple’s flagship handset. Will you yield to temptation and pay what’s likely to be <a href="https://go.skimresources.com?id=111346X1569486&xs=1&url=https://www.trendforce.com/news/2026/09/04/news-apples-iphone-18-lineup-takes-shape-prices-seen-rising-10-20-foldable-may-start-above-us2000/&xcust=1-0-3228054-1-0-0-0-0&sref=https://www.macworld.com/article/3228054/surprise-and-shine-apple-event-live-blog-iphone-18-pro-folding-duo-airpods.html" rel="nofollow" data-subtag="1-0-3228054-1-0-0-0-0" data-domain-name="trendforce" target="_blank">more than $2,000</a> for Apple’s first foldable smartphone?</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">One commenter on <a href="https://go.skimresources.com?id=111346X1569486&xs=1&url=https://www.youtube.com/shorts/DZ7_ZyBAOVo&xcust=1-0-3228054-1-0-0-0-0&sref=https://www.macworld.com/article/3228054/surprise-and-shine-apple-event-live-blog-iphone-18-pro-folding-duo-airpods.html" rel="nofollow" data-subtag="1-0-3228054-1-0-0-0-0" data-domain-name="youtube" target="_blank">our YouTube channel</a> is leaning towards no.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“If I was purchasing an iPhone and an iPad at the same time, then I would consider the Fold as it might work out cheaper than buying two separate devices,” writes <strong>christopherclarke6184</strong>. “But I am happy with my iPad M4 and iPhone 17 Pro Max so won’t be upgrading for a while… unless Apple has something special I may need. I’ll still be watching the show, though.”</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Apple will be hoping for strong interest from the early adopter crowd, but given that this is an entirely new market for the company and a very high price, moderate sales may be enough in the short term.</p>

<p class="wp-block-paragraph">One big difference this year is that the main host will be Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, rather than Tim Cook. Ternus is a relative unknown to members of the public, and Apple fans will be keen to see how he handles hosting duties. Will he be a showman, like Steve Jobs? Quietly professional, like Cook? Or something new and unique to himself?</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">That’s not to say we’ve got no idea how he’ll carry himself in a presentation. As head of hardware Ternus spoke at multiple keynotes and product launches in the past, including the iPhone reveal last fall. His manner was very positive, with lots of superlatives, while being unafraid to delve into technical detail. But acting as main host is a different assignment, so we may see a new side to him on Wednesday.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In the meantime, read Alex Blake’s <a href="https://www.macworld.com/article/3120377/john-ternus-is-the-perfect-ceo-for-this-apple-era.html">piece on the new boss,</a> in which he describes Ternus as “the perfect CEO for this Apple era.”</p>

What surprise?</h3>

<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Apple has given this week’s showcase the tagline “Surprise and Shine.” But what’s the big surprise? Apple’s September events are among its most predictable, almost always revolving around new iPhones and new Apple Watches, and sometimes new AirPods.</p>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li>September 2025: iPhones, Apple Watches, AirPods</li>



<li>September 2024: iPhones, Apple Watches, AirPods</li>



<li>September 2023: iPhones, Apple Watches</li>



<li>September 2022: iPhones, Apple Watches, AirPods</li>



<li>September 2021: iPhones, Apple Watches, iPads</li>
</ul>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Is John Ternus going to spring a surprise in 2026? After asking this question on <a href="https://go.skimresources.com?id=111346X1569486&xs=1&url=https://www.tiktok.com/@macworld.com/video/7681381857459588383&xcust=1-0-3228054-1-0-0-0-0&sref=https://www.macworld.com/article/3228054/surprise-and-shine-apple-event-live-blog-iphone-18-pro-folding-duo-airpods.html" rel="nofollow" data-subtag="1-0-3228054-1-0-0-0-0" data-domain-name="tiktok" target="_blank">TikTok</a> we’re unconvinced by the idea of an Apple alarm clock (sorry), but another reader’s proposal of a “tabletop Pixar light robot personal assistant with Siri” is a little more plausible. That sounds a lot like the rumored <a href="https://www.macworld.com/article/3201176/apples-big-siri-ai-powered-smart-home-hub-is-nearly-here.html">smart-home hub</a> which Apple has been working on for years, and could make an appearance this week. It could even turn up as One More Thing at the end and make for a fun encore.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">But ultimately the most likely outcome is that, as far as Apple is concerned, the widely expected <a href="https://www.macworld.com/article/2629813/iphone-ultra-folding-design-price-specs-release-date.html">foldable iPhone</a> counts as the surprise. To those of us who live in the Apple rumor bubble the iPhone Ultra (or iPhone Fold) now looks like virtually a sure thing for Wednesday’s presentation, but to the wider community it’s far less well known. And officially, of course, it doesn’t even exist. Surprise!</p>

<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Apple loves to launch at least one new color for each iPhone generation. Partly this allows the company to prune the colors which sold poorly the year before and experiment with alternatives, but the main advantage is that it allows customers to show off the fact they’ve got a new phone, even if the design is otherwise the same. Those who bought the iPhone 17 Pro in Cosmic Orange last year got some major bragging rights.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Perhaps surprisingly, the wildly popular Cosmic Orange is expected to be dropped from the range this year. The two new finishes are a little less garish: a dark-red/burgundy wine color, expected to be branded as Dark Cherry, and a light blue. Macworld <a href="https://www.macworld.com/article/3116701/iphone-18-pro-colors-revealed-exclusive-look-at-apples-2026-models.html">exclusively revealed these colors</a> in the summer.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">If you’d like to see more of the new finishes, take a look at <a href="https://www.macworld.com/article/3228523/iphone-18-pro-video-leak-appears-to-confirm-blue-and-dark-cherry-color-options.html">this leaked video</a>, which appears to show demo models of the iPhone 18 Pro (in blue) and 18 Pro Max (in Dark Cherry).</p>
